power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Although neurodivergent people can achieve high levels of academic and vocational training in the same professions as others, they remain un-and under-employed; this is in part due to the "wickedness" of the problem.

To address the complexity we convened a group of neurodivergent lived experience and employment experts to 1) define which problems in neurodiversity and skilled employment are most urgent to address; 2) create actionable strategies with potential leverage for generating the desired employment outcomes.
We used qualitative methods from the systems thinking field: Soft Systems Methodology, futures visioning and SWOT analysis, and Group Model Building (system dynamics).

The workshops resulted in identifying intervention leverage between organizational psychology constructs of employee wellbeing, workplace climate, and mutually beneficial workplace relationships, in conjunction with a new disability stress construct, rather than specific skills building or remediation of disability characteristics.

Reaching a future in which neurodivergent people love their jobs will take education, resources, champions from the outside and inside, universal access, paradigm shifts, infrastructure, and recognition of individual and social complexity.

We recommend examining the organizational psychology literature for adaptable interventions; focusing on peer support; leveraging emerging technology to manage complexity; and supporting supervisor behavior change based on authentic understanding.

Although neurodivergent (Autistic, ADHDer, autDHDer, Touretter, Dyslexic, Mad, etc.) people can achieve high levels of academic and vocational training in the same range of professions as others, they remain un-and under-employed even compared to people with other disabilities, particularly in skilled jobs (i.e., jobs requiring more than a few weeks of training to master).

Exact statistics for the U.S. remain elusive for reasons including the aggregation of disability type and job level in national reporting and a historic lack of research on neurodivergent adult employment.

However, based on aggregate statistics 1, 2 ; qualitative information from people with lived experience 3, 4 ; studies from comparable countries outside of the U.S. 5 ; and, discourse in both the business 6 and neurodiversity communities 7 , there is strong reason to believe that skilled employment imbalances exist.
text.formatted: However, based on aggregate statistics <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> ; qualitative information from people with lived experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> ; studies from comparable countries outside of the U.S. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> ; and, discourse in both the business <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> and neurodiversity communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> , there is strong reason to believe that skilled employment imbalances exist.

text.text: In recent decades, a plethora of programs have emerged to address these imbalances; however, solutions have had limited impact, particularly in skilled settings outside of information technology.

Typing "neurodiversity employment" into a search engine will produce hundreds of neurodiversity at work programs, articles on neurodivergent advantages in technology, tips for employers, and academic centers dedicated to the issue.
However, broad imbalances persist in skilled settings even as these interventions proliferate.

The reasons for this are multiple, including 1) a focus on unskilled jobs; 2) when skilled, a focus on technology jobs in wellresourced corporations leaving out the majority with training, interest, or talent in any other industry; 3) a focus on autism that excludes other forms of neurodivergence or multiply disabled autistic people; 4) tying programs to services when many fall through service gaps, particularly if they do not have intellectual disability or are managing their mental health conditions; 5) the conceptualization and direction of programs and services from outside the neurodiversity community; and, 6) the assumptions of a homogenous view of neurodivergence.
Despite the potential value of existing solutions for the subpopulations they serve, these solutions, in their current state, are insufficient even in aggregate to address the broader problem.
There is good reason for the narrow scope and large number of solutions.

Neurodiversity and skilled employment, like many problems in policy and public health, is a "wicked problem"-it has such a high degree of complexity that it lacks clarity both in terms of its formulation and its solution 8 .
text.formatted: Neurodiversity and skilled employment, like many problems in policy and public health, is a "wicked problem"-it has such a high degree of complexity that it lacks clarity both in terms of its formulation and its solution <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: Dimensions of complexity include the 1) dynamics of intense social stigma, 2) heterogenous nature of the population, 3) interdisciplinary nature of the domain, 4) evolving context of employment, and 5) high variance in real-world employment settings.

Narrowing the scope (e.g., to unskilled positions for transition-age autistic youth receiving services, or to highly controlled partnerships with technology corporations) is a way to reduce the complexity and make the problem less wicked-albeit at the cost of neglecting the majority of the problem space and population.

The proliferation of narrow solutions is symptomatic of both struggles with complexity and the characteristic of wicked problems that whomever defines the problem and they do so determines its possible solutions 9.
text.formatted: The proliferation of narrow solutions is symptomatic of both struggles with complexity and the characteristic of wicked problems that whomever defines the problem and they do so determines its possible solutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref>.

text.text: To address the complexity of the problem and further our long-term aim of improving skilled employment outcomes for neurodivergent people, we took a systems thinking and communityengaged approach using methods designed for wicked problems.

Our project had two objectives: 1) to define which problems in neurodiversity and skilled employment are most urgent to address and their desired outcomes/goals for intervention and 2) to create actionable strategies with potential leverage for generating the desired employment outcomes.

This project used a Participatory Action Research (PAR) 10 approach, in which 1) all members of the research team are also members of the research's target population, and 2) the research should generate change.
text.formatted: This project used a Participatory Action Research (PAR) <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> approach, in which 1) all members of the research team are also members of the research's target population, and 2) the research should generate change.

text.text: Specifically, it promotes lived experience as knowledge that is just as valid as academic expertise, and it employs the systematic inquiry of science to create realworld change that benefits the neurodiversity community and population.
Systems thinking is an approach to holistic inquiry with roots in pragmatism and operations research during World War II 11, 12 .
text.formatted: Systems thinking is an approach to holistic inquiry with roots in pragmatism and operations research during World War II <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: As a reaction to the non-mechanistic (i.e., unpredictable, heterogeneous, non-physical) and deeply nonlinear (i.e., feedback-driven) nature of complex socio-technical systems-which makes them difficult or impossible to understand and control using traditional reductionist science-systems thinking is a way to work with complex phenomena without breaking them into component parts.
It is a means to, essentially, "see both the forest and the trees" 13 .
text.formatted: It is a means to, essentially, "see both the forest and the trees" <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: As skilled employment for neurodivergent people is a massively complex domain, this project uses systems thinking methodologies for holistic inquiry.
We used three qualitative methodologies from the systems thinking field to define the problem and identify outcomes: Soft Systems Methodology, futures visioning, and Group Model Building.
Soft Systems Methodology (SSM) generates action plans to address problems in situations where both the problem and its solutions are ill-defined 12 .
text.formatted: Soft Systems Methodology (SSM) generates action plans to address problems in situations where both the problem and its solutions are ill-defined <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: It is completed collaboratively by a small group of stakeholders, and comprises seven steps which can be used independently or in various combinations 12 .
text.formatted: It is completed collaboratively by a small group of stakeholders, and comprises seven steps which can be used independently or in various combinations <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: The steps are 1) determine a scope for the problem; 2) express it with a rich picture; 3) formulate "root definitions," or statements of purpose that describe the problem space and transformation in the format of "what to do, how to do it, why to do it;" 4) build a conceptual model of activities to achieve the transformation; 5) compare the model to the real world; 6) identify desirable and feasible actions; and 7) create a plan for action.

Futures visioning 14 is a futures thinking method designed to 1) frame the past and present; 2) imagine desirable futures; and 3) reconcile where we are with where we want to be (i.e., the futures vision).
text.formatted: Futures visioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> is a futures thinking method designed to 1) frame the past and present; 2) imagine desirable futures; and 3) reconcile where we are with where we want to be (i.e., the futures vision).

text.text: For the first two futures visioning activities, we imagined we had achieved the transformations in the root definitions (from the SSM), and then answered the questions: 1.
What have we achieved?
Who are our stakeholders and how have they benefited from what we've done?
What are we most pleased about?
What have we put in place to make sure we can sustain over time?
How are we measuring progress and success?
Is there anything we still need to do?
What are the challenges we face now?
For the third futures visioning activity we conducted a SWOT (Strength, Weakness, Opportunity, Threat) Analysis, using the categories and themes from the futures visioning as input 14.
text.formatted: For the third futures visioning activity we conducted a SWOT (Strength, Weakness, Opportunity, Threat) Analysis, using the categories and themes from the futures visioning as input <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref>.

text.text: System dynamics is the study of feedback and control, and its methodologies focus on modeling complex, nonlinear systems in holistic (i.e., non-reductionist) ways that can enhance understanding and capacity for intervention in these situations. 11 Group Model Building (GMB) generates collaborative qualitative system dynamics models called Causal Loop Diagrams (CLDs).
text.formatted: System dynamics is the study of feedback and control, and its methodologies focus on modeling complex, nonlinear systems in holistic (i.e., non-reductionist) ways that can enhance understanding and capacity for intervention in these situations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> Group Model Building (GMB) generates collaborative qualitative system dynamics models called Causal Loop Diagrams (CLDs).

text.text: The method enables experts with no training in system dynamics to develop CLDs with the facilitation of skilled modelers 15.
text.formatted: The method enables experts with no training in system dynamics to develop CLDs with the facilitation of skilled modelers <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref>.

text.text: The first two phases of GMB are 1) identifying the problem to model and 2) planning the workshop with facilitators.
The third phase comprises: 1.
Brainstorming the "nouns" or ideas that function as nouns involved in the problem.
Identifying feedback relationships among nouns to create "seed" CLD structures to serve as starting points for group discussion.
Introducing feedback thinking (i.e., thinking in terms of simultaneous mutual influences rather than linear cause and effect) to the expert group.
Generating the completed CLD structures from the seed structures through group discussion.
Editing the structures into a cohesive model and validating the model by comparing it to real-world data or known theory.
Qualitatively analyzing policies and interventions.
Our paradigmatic lens for workshop analyses combined aspects of constructivism with a critical realist ontology 16 , critical 17 , and transformative paradigms 18.
text.formatted: Our paradigmatic lens for workshop analyses combined aspects of constructivism with a critical realist ontology <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> , critical <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> , and transformative paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref>.

text.text: The project used a participatory action research approach 10 with seven experts (including the Principal Investigator, DMR) who 1) have lived experience of neurodivergence and neurodiversity culture; 2) have professional expertise relevant to employment; 3) represent demographic heterogeneity (race, gender, geographic region, industry, education).
text.formatted: The project used a participatory action research approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> with seven experts (including the Principal Investigator, DMR) who 1) have lived experience of neurodivergence and neurodiversity culture; 2) have professional expertise relevant to employment; 3) represent demographic heterogeneity (race, gender, geographic region, industry, education).

text.text: Our collective neurodivergence includes autism, ADHD, learning disabilities, psychiatric disabilities, sensory processing disabilities, and mobility disabilities.

Our collective professional expertise includes employee resource group leadership, disability employment policy, peer support, employee management, product accessibility, clinical practice, academic research, industrial process analysis, and disability service systems across technology, research, arts, policy, academic, and health industries.

Our PAR group collaborated with two systems science PhD students, KA and JC, and our research assistant PI who provided facilitation and support for the Group Model Building workshops and the causal loop diagramming.
WW, an experienced modeler with an outside perspective, assisted with CLD analysis.
This study took place in the U.S. and focused on U.S.-based employment systems for reasons of feasibility.
While this study was a systematic inquiry (i.e., research), it did not involve human subjects or population sampling.

We collected data in 8 remote workshops on Zoom: 1) Soft Systems Methodology steps 1 and 2; 2) Soft Systems Methodology step 3; 3) Futures visioning; 4) SWOT analysis; 5) GMB, which also served as SSM step 4, 6) initial leverage identification; 7) SSM step 5 using the final GMB output; and 8) SSM steps 6 and 7 using an Ease/Benefit matrix.
DMR facilitated all workshops except the rich picture workshop, led by an expert in visual facilitation, and the GMB workshop, which KA, JC, and PI facilitated.
For all workshops, the team provided information verbally, in text chat, and, when applicable, by writing on shared whiteboards and documents.
For workshop 1, the visual facilitator created a live record of our discussion by drawing on whiteboards.
They prompted the team first to discuss the current situation of neurodivergence at work, and then to discuss the ideal situation.
For workshop 2, we collected data during the workshop in a shared document structured with the CATWOE (Client, Actor, Transformation, Worldview, Owner, Environment) framework 12 .
text.formatted: For workshop 2, we collected data during the workshop in a shared document structured with the CATWOE (Client, Actor, Transformation, Worldview, Owner, Environment) framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: The document remained open after the workshop for team members to add additional ideas.
For workshops 3 and 4, we collected data live on shared whiteboards that DMR set up with the futures vision questions and the SWOT grid.
For workshop 5, the GMB workshop, DMR introduced the team to feedback thinking.
We then developed the models through group discussion.
KA facilitated the discussion while JC updated the structures on a Miro board and PI took additional notes on ideas to integrate into the structures after the meeting.
Workshop 6 focused on identifying initial leverage.

We collected data through live discussion on a Zoom whiteboard formatted with headings for each high-level category of leverage in Meadow's leverage framework: physical events, information/patterns of behavior, social/system structure, and mental models/paradigm 19 .
text.formatted: We collected data through live discussion on a Zoom whiteboard formatted with headings for each high-level category of leverage in Meadow's leverage framework: physical events, information/patterns of behavior, social/system structure, and mental models/paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: Workshop 7 presented the edited, verified CLD, updated the original root definitions based on what we learned from our system dynamics modeling, and performed an initial analysis of actions that could trigger leverage based on the model through discussion of several starter theories of change synthesized by DMR.
This provided the conceptual model for SSM step 5.
We collected data through discussion on a FreeForm board.

Workshop 8 presented a draft logic model based on the theories of change, areas of leverage, and additional brainstorming, to create an Ease/Benefit Matrix of potential solutions ("ease" being similar to "cost" but more holistic in scope).
We collected data through live discussion on a Zoom whiteboard formatted as an Ease/Benefit Matrix.

For the rich picture, the visual facilitation included frequent check-ins to verify the pictures correctly captured the discussion (i.e., data collection, processing, analysis, and trustworthiness occurred simultaneously).
For workshop 2, DMR used the information in the shared CATWOE document and rich pictures to create a first draft of the root definitions.
This involved following the SSM procedure for casting the data into the format of "Do P by Q to achieve R," where PQR answers the questions, "What?
How?
Why?"
or "do what by how to achieve the why."
This defines the transformation as a purposeful activity.
DMR presented the draft root definitions to the team, who memberchecked 20 and refined them in a shared document and through feedback during a meeting.
text.formatted: DMR presented the draft root definitions to the team, who memberchecked <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> and refined them in a shared document and through feedback during a meeting.

text.text: DMR edited the root definitions later based on what we'd learned from our examination of dynamics and leverage, which the group again member-checked and refined.
For workshops 3 and 4, DMR conducted a content analysis 21 of the discussion to synthesize it into categories and themes and member-checked them with the group for trustworthiness 22 .
text.formatted: For workshops 3 and 4, DMR conducted a content analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> of the discussion to synthesize it into categories and themes and member-checked them with the group for trustworthiness <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: We removed one category from the SWOT content analysis-strengths related to the visibility of disability in employment-after our examination of dynamics and leverage revised our assumptions about it (it has dynamics that can lead to worse outcomes and othering which make its role both ambiguous and less impactive than the items we retained).

System dynamics modeling requires verification to be rigorous, and after the GMB and leverage workshops 5-7, DMR located relevant literature and real-world data with which to triangulate, adjust, and reconcile the CLDs, as described in Sterman 23 .
text.formatted: System dynamics modeling requires verification to be rigorous, and after the GMB and leverage workshops 5-7, DMR located relevant literature and real-world data with which to triangulate, adjust, and reconcile the CLDs, as described in Sterman <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: The verification process with existing literature allowed us to organize our many structures and leverage points under existing occupational theories.
We also used member-checking with the group periodically during model development and to confirm the final models presented here.

Objective 1: Define which problems in neurodiversity and skilled employment are most urgent to address and their desired outcomes SSM Steps 1 and 2: Prior to starting our workshops, we had identified the problem of poor employment outcomes for neurodivergent people with skilled training.
Figures 1 and 2 show the rich pictures produced during our first SSM workshop.
text.formatted: Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> and <ref type="figure">2</ref> show the rich pictures produced during our first SSM workshop.

text.text: Figure 2: Rich Picture of the Desired Landscape SSM Step 3: Our initial draft of root definitions listed transformations related to accessible workplaces; financial/personal/professional safety; job fit; employee wellness; fair employment; and sense of acceptance, value, and community at work.
After completing our system dynamics processes, including verification with existing theory, we refined them to those reported below.

Transform employee well-being by providing tools to employees and employers for aligning person-job-organization fit, supporting healthy boundaries and advocacy, supporting employee mental health and self-care, and supporting neurodivergent needs holistically at and outside of work.

Transform workplace climate by providing tools to employees for coping with challenging workplace cultures and to employers for tailoring organizational support for employee autonomy, structure, reward, warmth, support, and accommodations.

Transform disability pressure from a harmful dynamic to a protective dynamic by connecting employees with disability community, identity, validation, shared communication burden, and peer support tools for coping, positive psychology, and resilience.
Transform workplace interactions into mutually beneficial relationships that support innovation, productivity, and organizational goals by enacting the prior three transformations.
In our desired future , Neurodivergent people love their work!
Employees and their communities are healthy.
There is a culturally ingrained, holistic, and accurate understanding of neurodivergence and the needs of neurodivergent employees, which also extends to other employee characteristics.
Higher-order impacts emerge in innovation, policy, practice, and paradigms that benefit the public.
We need to move beyond awareness campaigns, mandatory disability trainings, and public service announcements.
Neurotypical people need to learn more about neurodivergent processing, skill sets, and behavior, as well as how to have better empathy for neurodivergent people.
Organizational leaders and the public need to better understand the benefits of a workforce that includes both neurodivergent and neurotypical employees.
Educational resources need to be clear, accurate, include neurodivergent perspectives, and target a variety of audiences (e.g., management, co-workers, service providers, clinicians, the public).

While neurodivergent people's lived experiences are foundational to education, those who already carry a substantial burden, especially those with additional lived experiences, should not be asked, nor expected, to educate, and we need to be prepared to recognize and diffuse pressure for them to do so.
To create educational resources, we need more open conversations across stakeholders that center neurodivergent voices and priorities.
We need the federal, industrial, and foundational entities that provide funding and resources to understand, develop, and carry out the steps needed to create the transformations.
Consideration of both systems-level and individual-level resource distribution needs to happen when allocating funding and resources.
For example, by distributing money and resources to neurodivergent people to meet short-term needs, while supporting research programs to develop, test, and implement long-term solutions.
These resources must reach, or at least benefit, neurodivergent people, not just the institutions that hold them.
Given how far we remain from the vision despite recent progress, we need champions from outside the neurodiversity community, especially with systems-level power.
This includes buy-in from organizational leadership; champions in policy, service systems, research, education, and clinical practice; and allies who advance the priorities of the community.
These champions need to use their power directly to advocate for change and indirectly to create opportunities for neurodivergent people.
We need to continue advancing neurodivergent people into positions of power within employment systems who are willing and able to do the extra work of ambassadors.
This includes more neurodivergent people in politics, organizational leadership, management, employment services, research, and education.
We need to use the internal strengths of our community to provide peer mentorship and peer support for and at work.
To do that, we need to recognize both the substantial value of peer support and mentorship, and the extra burden of being a peer support specialist or mentor.
We need to act on that recognition by providing essential support and improved financial compensation to peer workers and better understand and address peer burnout.

We need to hear from more voices within our community-including those with overlapping characteristics and those most impacted-to guide external and internal champions and provide more comprehensive community leadership.
There are likely many neurodivergent workers in skilled positions who do not know they are neurodivergent or do not have a diagnosis.
Even for those with a diagnosis, the barriers to requesting accommodations may be too high.
Universal access that includes adjustments for neurodivergent processing has the potential to meet the needs of these employees.

Employment outcomes might also improve for neurotypical employees who would benefit from the same adjustments (i.e., "the curb cut effect" for communication, sensory processing, and cognition rather than mobility), though access should not be predicated on this.
When implementing universal access, we must attend to nuances and under-served access needs.

For example, we need to preserve systems for supported decision-making, provide pathways to communication for all, be responsive to conflicting accommodations, and not be dogmatic about the ways neurodivergence can express itself.
How close we are to our vision depends on whether socio-political climates keep improving for neurodiversity framing and acceptance or keep deteriorating.
This moment is unusual in that loud signals are happening in both directions.
We need to continue looking for creative ways to shift paradigms toward acceptance.
For example, by seeking systems that interact with neurodiversity and employment and are signaling a stronger push toward improvement, such clinical practice, clinical education, and research.
Another is by navigating ideological minefields and echo chambers to collaborate meaningfully with people with conflicting paradigms, incorporating their ideas without compromising the vision.

For example, by learning why some employers are uncomfortable hiring neurodivergent employees or asking people who wish to be cured of their neurodivergence for input on employment service interventions.
Lastly, supporting paradigm shifts that value workers more or give workers more power (e.g., employee-owned business models) could help support transformations for neurodivergent workers too.
We need holistic coordination between statewide and local service systems, systems navigation, education and training systems, and human resource systems.

The current silos between systems hurt neurodivergent people in multiple ways, from arguing who pays for someone who is both autistic and bipolar to failing to create an effective or sustainable transition between higher education support systems and employment support systems.
Service gaps need filling for all neurodivergent people.
Further, we need to analyze and modify employment policies and programs, even those designed to be helpful, for ways they might undermine successful employment of neurodivergent people.
For example, those that perpetuate sub-minimum wages, or that make it impossible for skilled people to work without loss of critical services.
We also need to remove silos between neurodivergence and other demographic factors involved in employment imbalances.

Neurodivergent people have the same range of characteristics as neurotypical people, some of which can create better opportunities while others can accumulate barriers over time (e.g., socio-economic status, geographical location, race, documentation status, gender, sexuality, co-occurring disability, religion, etc.).
We need to attend to within-group employment imbalances and employee needs while we attend to between-group (i.e., neurodivergent-neurotypical) imbalances.
We need to recognize that some neurodivergent individuals are closer to our vision than others and include everyone as we move toward the future.

text.text: CLDs are read by following the arrows around loops.
A positive arrow means the variables influence each other in the same way; a negative arrow that they influence each other in opposite ways.

Loop labels indicate the essence of the loop, its direction, and a polarity-does it create a Reinforcing loop which exhibits exponential behavior or a Balancing loop which exhibits asymptotic behavior?
Variables external to loops but influencing them are shown with a light, dotted line.
Two external variables-workplace culture gap and socio-political climate regarding neurodivergence-influence disability pressure.
Workplace culture gap is the difference between the norms of a workplace and the needs of a neurodivergent worker.
For example, in a company with a history of valuing and rewarding neurotypical social behavior, the gap would be large, and disability pressure also large.
However, a workplace culture where social activities are optional and whimsy encouraged might have a smaller gap, and disability pressure would also be smaller.
These variables are important but difficult to predict or impact, as they are entrenched (workplace culture) or volatile (socio-political climate).
This reinforcing loop describes the feedback between disability pressure and workplace climate.
As a vicious cycle, it describes the situation in which as pressure increases so do negative feelings about work, which increases pressure.
As a virtuous cycle, it describes a situation in which as workplace climate improves, pressure goes down, and the employee has an improved perception of their workplace.
This balancing loop describes the feedback between disability pressure and adjustments to person-job-organization fit.
The greater the pressure, the more adjustment needed; the more adjustments, the lower the pressure.
The ability to adjust, however, is regulated by the accessibility capacity of the person, job, and organization, which limits what is possible.
This balancing loop (long dashes) describes the feedback between person-joborganization fit, workplace climate, and disability pressure.
Providing adjustments to improve fit improves climate, which reduces pressure and the number of adjustments needed.
It's regulated by both the workplace culture gap and socio-political climate influences on disability pressure, and the accessibility capacity on person-job-organization fit.
How much an employee's needs are accommodated impacts workplace climate and the amount of disability pressure they are under at work.
A sense of belonging or workplace community is more likely when the employee feels supported by measurable adjustments to meet their needs.
Employee wellbeing is regulated by the external variable of the services gap.
This includes not just services related to employment, but other services the employee needs to be well in their life.
For example, assistance with instrumental activities like housekeeping and shopping, access to transportation, and therapy.
The more unmet needs an employee has, the worse their wellbeing, regardless of how well the job is going.
This limits even the best workplace dynamics; however, it also suggests how employment outcomes might be improved through indirect means.
This balancing loop (blue/lighter shaded) involves the variables of mutually beneficial relations, disability pressure, person-job-organization fit, and employee wellbeing.
Improved relations reduce disability pressure and improve job fit, which improves employee wellbeing.
Healthy employees are more capable of having healthy, mutually beneficial relations with their supervisors, co-workers, and overall job tasks.
The better the relations, the less the disability pressure, the better the person-job-organization fit, and the better the employee health.
These are known factors in innovation, productivity, and job stability (see Discussion).
The workplace culture, socio-political climate, accessibility capacity, and services gap, however, regulate how far this dynamic can reach.
Feedback impacting overall employment outcomes R² Employment outcomes.
This long outside reinforcing loop (bold) around the entire structure involves the variables of disability pressure, workplace climate, employee wellbeing, and mutually beneficial relations.
If acting as a vicious cycle leading to poor employment outcomes, increased disability pressure leads to decreased workplace climate and poorer employee wellbeing.
Poorer wellbeing leads to less mutually beneficial relations, which increases disability pressure.
Eventually, a breaking point comes and the employee cannot sustain.

If acting as a virtuous cycle, lower disability pressure leads to a better workplace climate, increased employee wellbeing, and increased mutually beneficial relations, which lowers disability pressure and leads to successful employment.
We identified the major points of leverage within disability pressure, workplace climate, employee wellbeing, and mutually beneficial relations.
Minor points of leverage exist in accessibility and person-job-organization fit.

Although policy had been a major part of our GMB session and structures, we ultimately placed it outside of the system due to its capriciousness and surface impact (i.e., it influences the external variables of workplace culture, socio-political climate, accessibility capacity, and services gap but rarely creates deep structural change resilient to policy reversals or environmental changes).

text.text: The following are the highest impact solutions or plans for action from our ease/benefit analysis, in order of ease.
• Peer mentor and peer support resources, both static and live, including content related to employee wellness, positive psychology, and strategies for managing difficult work situations.

• Accommodation decision and solution aids based on functional needs and sensitive to workplace culture, climate, industry, job characteristics, and employee characteristics, including disclosure risk.
• Supervisor behavior change tools for supporting neurodivergent employees, targeted toward supervisors motivated to change (e.g., adapting the VSST Intervention for veterans 24 ).
text.formatted: • Supervisor behavior change tools for supporting neurodivergent employees, targeted toward supervisors motivated to change (e.g., adapting the VSST Intervention for veterans <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> ).

text.text: • Troubleshooting and solution aids for employee-job-organization fit based on functional need and sensitive to workplace culture, climate, industry, job characteristics, and employee characteristics including disclosure risk.

• Work pragmatics translation tools that assist with interpretation, scripting, and communicating with neurotypical supervisors, co-workers, or clients and is sensitive to the workplace culture, climate, and nature of the industry and job, and a reverse translator for neurotypicals to understand neurodivergent employees.

Taking a participatory action research and systems thinking approach to the problem of employment imbalances for skilled neurodivergent people resulted in a focus on transforming employee wellbeing, workplace environments and climates, disability pressure, and enhancing workplace innovation rather than specific skills building or remediation of disability characteristics.

Doing this will take education, resources and funding, champions from the outside, champions from the inside, universal access and accessibility, paradigm shifts, infrastructure, and recognition of individual and social complexity.

Actionable courses of intervention include increased focus on interactive and passive peer support and mentoring that targets the areas of transformation; leveraging emerging technology to support accommodations, job fit, and workplace communication including in situations where disability disclosure is not feasible; and supporting supervisor behavior change based on authentic understanding neurodivergence at work rather than through policy demands.
Neurodivergent people must be involved in developing these solutions from a holistic perspective.
This includes activities surrounding solution building, as defining the problem, designing the solution, and determining evaluation and assessment criteria.
The areas of transformation in our root definitions map to known multidimensional constructs in the literature.

From the organizational literature, employee wellbeing includes health and safety both within and outside the workplace 25 ; the dimensions proposed by Attipoe 26 in particular, reflect our discussions of the interconnected facets of physical health, mental health, emotional health, job satisfaction, work/life balance, and overall quality of life.
text.formatted: From the organizational literature, employee wellbeing includes health and safety both within and outside the workplace <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> ; the dimensions proposed by Attipoe <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> in particular, reflect our discussions of the interconnected facets of physical health, mental health, emotional health, job satisfaction, work/life balance, and overall quality of life.

text.text: Workplace climate, the perception of the work environment both individually and collectively, can be conceived as an outward expression of workplace culture, the ingrained norms of the workplace 27 .
text.formatted: Workplace climate, the perception of the work environment both individually and collectively, can be conceived as an outward expression of workplace culture, the ingrained norms of the workplace <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> .

text.text: While workplace climate theory is still unfolding, the climate constructs of leader support and facilitation, role stress and harmony, job challenge and autonomy, and workgroup cooperation, warmth, and friendliness described in James, Choi, Ko, McNeil, Minton, Wright, Kim 28 and those in the workplace climate scale developed by Patterson, West, Shackleton, Dawson, Lawthom, Maitlis, Robinson, Wallace 29 map well to our discussions.
text.formatted: While workplace climate theory is still unfolding, the climate constructs of leader support and facilitation, role stress and harmony, job challenge and autonomy, and workgroup cooperation, warmth, and friendliness described in James, Choi, Ko, McNeil, Minton, Wright, Kim <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> and those in the workplace climate scale developed by Patterson, West, Shackleton, Dawson, Lawthom, Maitlis, Robinson, Wallace 29 map well to our discussions.

text.text: While culture takes a long time to change because of its roots in historical norms, climate is more amenable to short-term intervention and, over time, can shift the paradigms of culture by reinforcing new norms.
The disability pressure construct is not directly present in the literature, but it maps in part to the model proposed by Meyer 30 .
text.formatted: The disability pressure construct is not directly present in the literature, but it maps in part to the model proposed by Meyer <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> .

text.text: Meyer's model shows how general stressors, unfair treatment based on personal characteristics, and the expectation of that unfair treatment can lead to poor health outcomes.
Simultaneously, it shows that sense of community and identity related to those same characteristics is protective at both individual and community levels, which can lead to good health outcomes.
The model is 1) unidirectional rather showing feedback; and 2) not specific to disability.
We are currently developing a feedback model of disability pressure.

Critically, employee wellbeing, workplace climate, person-job-organization fit, and heterogeneity of workplaces are all known to influence productivity and innovation. 26, 27, [31] [32] [33] That these known constructs and relationships emerged organically from our workshops should, on one hand, be no surprise, as neurodivergent people are engaging in the same occupational systems as the general population.
text.formatted: Critically, employee wellbeing, workplace climate, person-job-organization fit, and heterogeneity of workplaces are all known to influence productivity and innovation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> That these known constructs and relationships emerged organically from our workshops should, on one hand, be no surprise, as neurodivergent people are engaging in the same occupational systems as the general population.

text.text: However, the development of interventions from this literature to improve employment outcomes for neurodivergent people is sparse, and interventions in companies that target these constructs are not improving overall outcomes for neurodivergent employees.

This suggests that there is a large, unexplored literature to draw from in intervention development, while known interventions from this literature likely need adaptation to be effective for neurodivergent employees.

Notably, our work did not define the problem or its solutions in terms of the types of individuallevel behaviors most often targeted by disability employment interventions and policies; for example jobseekers not behaving typically enough to pass a job interview, or businesses not having sufficient financial incentive to hire difficult employees.
Instead, we defined the problem in terms of breakdowns in the interconnected dimensions that drive broader employment outcomes for employees, businesses, and society.

For example, inadequate support for neurodivergent employee wellness, or supervisors unaware of how to create the kinds of relationships with their neurodivergent employees that lead to increased innovation and productivity.
This suggests a different set of actions for solution.

While neurodivergent people are increasingly included in employment research, to our knowledge no research to date has explicitly grounded itself in neurodivergent epistemology and defined the problems in employment outcomes fresh from that center, rather than by building on the existing work of neurotypical researchers.

Our findings have more in common with organizational interventions than with disability interventions, which both provides evidence of transferability of our ideas and a suggestion that taking an organizational approach rather than a medicalized approach could open new avenues for effective intervention.
Most importantly, our work shows the importance of centering the field in both the lived experience and professional expertise of neurodivergent people.
Peer support, peer mentoring, and participation in peer communities are both protective factors and effective interventions.

The substance use and early psychosis literature, in particular, has shown robust connections between peer engagement and improved outcomes 34 , and peer interventions are starting to be used within occupations that have a strong sense of community, like first responders 35 .
text.formatted: The substance use and early psychosis literature, in particular, has shown robust connections between peer engagement and improved outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref> , and peer interventions are starting to be used within occupations that have a strong sense of community, like first responders <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> .

text.text: Our work identified peer engagement as a key point of leverage for improving employment outcomes.

Despite this, peer support is less valued than other therapies, as evident by extreme pay imbalances (a peer support specialist in 2025 makes on average $20 per hour in Oregon, while an occupational therapist makes an average of $50).

Acknowledging the equivalence of academic education and lived experience, when combined with insight into how that experience interacts with surrounding systems, could help increase the perceived value of peers clinical practice.
Taking a systems thinking approach enabled a high-level and long-term view of how individual, organizational, and environmental components influence overall employment outcomes.

We conducted this research in the U.S. when the environment surrounding disability and employment is out of equilibrium, including an abrupt erosion of disability rights protections and policies and unusual levels of economic uncertainty.
However, we feel our findings and recommendations would have applied prior to the current disequilibrium.
The U.S. focus limits the transferability of findings to other countries.

While our expert group included multiple kinds of neurodivergence and personal characteristics, we did not have a full range of expertise; future work should also engage people with lived experience of Tourette's, OCD, and other common forms of neurodivergence, as well as with people who experience a broader range of demographic characteristics (e.g., age, geographic location, etc.).
 Explore adapting evidence-based interventions that target employee wellbeing, workplace climate, and employer/employee relationships for neurodivergent workers.

 Conduct efficacy research on tools the neurodiversity community has created for itself (e.g., Goblin Tools for pragmatics translation, https://goblin.tools)  Explore disability pressure and the role it plays in employment outcomes and wellbeing.
text.formatted:  Conduct efficacy research on tools the neurodiversity community has created for itself (e.g., Goblin Tools for pragmatics translation, <ref type="url" target="https://goblin.tools">https://goblin.tools</ref>)  Explore disability pressure and the role it plays in employment outcomes and wellbeing.

text.text:  Involve people with lived experience in defining intervention outcomes and developing interventions.
 Encourage interdisciplinary collaborations with organizational psychologists and others with expertise in business dynamics outside of medical and disability fields.

 Invest in business development to help entrepreneurs incorporate neurodivergent talent into their workforce from the start, as well as to support neurodivergent entrepreneurs who can model best-practices in neurodiversity-friendly business development.

 Find ways emerging technology can support solutions that are not tied to specific services, industries, or diagnoses; in particular, artificial intelligence may help manage heterogeneity in ways that were previously not possible.
 Support peer support specialists and peer strategies to lessen employee burden, reduce disability pressure, and promote employee wellbeing.
 Explore structural solutions that are not reliant on policy.

 Research why existing programs aren't moving outcomes, including assessments of scalability and focus (e.g., how can small, siloed programs that hit many of our recommendations such as Aspiritech (https://aspiritech.org) scale to reach a larger neurodivergent population and outside of technology).
text.formatted:  Research why existing programs aren't moving outcomes, including assessments of scalability and focus (e.g., how can small, siloed programs that hit many of our recommendations such as Aspiritech (<ref type="url" target="https://aspiritech.org">https://aspiritech.org</ref>) scale to reach a larger neurodivergent population and outside of technology).

text.text: To reduce imbalances for neurodivergent people in skilled employment, we recommend taking a systemic and disability-led approach to defining the problem and locating its many better solutions.

This project takes a step back from the current chaos to use systematic inquiry designed for situations of high complexity to define the problems that most urgently need addressing, determine what they might look like if resolved, understand the current state of the system that gives rise to them, identify the leverage within the system that could effectively generate change, and develop a holistic, data-informed, plan for action.
Critically, this project leverages the native innovation and expertise of the neurodiversity community itself to point toward the north star of, "We love our jobs!"
